subject: Secure ingress path options — PrivateLink vs peering vs site-to-site VPN

Subject: Secure ingress path options — PrivateLink vs peering vs site-to-site VPN

Hi Sam —

Great to chat this morning. Per our call, I wanted to capture the three connectivity patterns we typically recommend for Redwood Private deployments and ask a few clarifying questions so we can size and propose the right design for EdgeShift:

Options (high-level):
- AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints): least blast radius, fine-grained per-service access, recommended when you need strong isolation across customer accounts and want to avoid routing/prefix overlap. Latency typically slightly higher than peering; good for multi-account deployments.
- VPC Peering: lowest hop-count/latency for same-region VPC-to-VPC traffic; simple and cost-effective for steady east-west traffic but doesn’t scale transitively and becomes complex across many VPCs or cross-account topologies.
- Site-to-Site VPN (IPSec): recommended when you have on-prem or data-center workloads that must access Redwood over a managed tunnel. Works well for hybrid cases but adds latency and operational overhead; consider Direct Connect/ExpressRoute for high-throughput production links.

A few clarifying Qs from your infra answers so we can pick a primary + fallback path:
1) Expected sustained TPS and peak token throughput to the private endpoint (tokens/sec or requests/sec)?
2) Do you need cross-account access from multiple AWS accounts (EdgeShift staging/prod, partner accounts, etc.)?
3) Compliance constraints: do you require dedicated network paths (no shared AWS infra) or are strict ACLs on PrivateLink sufficient?
4) Any preference on egress costs being minimized vs absolute lowest latency?

I attached a short matrix that maps typical workloads to the recommended primary/fallback choice (connectivity_matrix.pdf). If you can share your network inventory export (VPCs, CIDRs, on-prem gateway IPs), we’ll sketch the exact configuration.

Proposed next steps:
- You send the network inventory (or just the CIDRs and accounts).
- Karthik to produce a one-page diagram + table showing tradeoffs and latency/cost estimates.
- Procurement: if we agree on PrivateLink or Dedicated Direct Connect, procurement will need a short SOW and network contact list.

Thanks — I’ll loop Karthik in for the topology recommendation once we have the inventory.

Priya —

Thanks for the summary and the matrix — super helpful. Quick answers below and I attached our network inventory export (network_inventory.xlsx):

1) Throughput: baseline ~600 reqs/min (avg), peaks up to ~5k reqs/min during batch runs; payloads average ~1.2 KB; tokenization on our side happens in batches.
2) Yes — we have two AWS accounts (edgeshift-prod, edgeshift-platform) that need access. We also plan to open access to a partner account later this year.
3) Compliance: we’re SOC2 Type II and need isolation for customer data stores. We’re OK with shared managed infra provided we can enforce ACLs + VPC endpoint policies.
4) Egress costs matter but SLA/latency matter more for inference (real-time features). If there’s a 10–20ms penalty for PrivateLink, we can tolerate it.

We’d prefer to avoid a complex mesh of peering across many VPCs. Happy to get your recommendation; procurement is CC’d — they’ll need estimated pricing and any network IPs for firewall rules.

Hi all —

Thanks for the inventory, Sam — useful. I ran a quick pass and sketched the recommendation in the attached PNG. Key points and concrete recommendation below.

Summary recommendation (short):
- Primary: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) from each EdgeShift account to Redwood Private service VPC. Rationale: gives per-account access control via endpoint policies, avoids CIDR collision complexity, and simplifies cross-account partner onboarding. Latency penalty is typically single-digit ms for same-region interface endpoints; given your tolerance this is acceptable.
- Fallback/accelerator: For the most latency-sensitive realtime path (if we see <50ms P95 targets unmet), add an optional peering link between edgeshift-prod and Redwood dedicated VPC for that bounded subset of traffic (requires strict routing controls and non-overlapping CIDRs). Use prefix-lists and route-table tags to keep scope limited.
- Hybrid/on-prem: For your on-prem or co-lo workloads, Site-to-Site VPN is appropriate as a stop-gap. For sustained high-throughput (<100s of MB/s) we should discuss Direct Connect; Redwood can support partner-hosted cross-connects under a Dedicated capacity plan.

Tradeoffs and operational notes:
- PrivateLink pros: simple security posture, no routing table churn, good for multi-account. Cons: per-endpoint ENI costs and slightly higher per-request latency and egress if traffic traverses managed VPC endpoints.
- Peering pros: minimal latency, no ENI overhead. Cons: non-transitive, scaling pain, requires strict CIDR management and can complicate cross-account partner onboarding.
- VPN pros: fast to stand up; good for hybrid. Cons: latency and jitter; not ideal for high-concurrency, low-latency inference workloads without Direct Connect.

Concrete next technical steps I propose:
1) We publish a short endpoint-policy example and sample SG rules for your Infra team (I’ll send this today).
2) We model cost delta (PrivateLink vs peering) for your expected throughput — estimate attached in the PNG.
3) If you want a hybrid low-latency pilot, we can stand up a peered link scoped to a single service subnet and run a two-week load test to validate P95s.

Risk mitigations:
- For ENI/PrivateLink explosion, use a single regional endpoint per account plus ALB/Service mapping on Redwood side to minimize ENI count.
- For peering-related operational risk, require an automated CIDR check and maintain route prefix-lists in Terraform to prevent accidental overlap.

I’ll follow up with the example endpoint policy and a short firewall whitelist (CIDRs and ports) so procurement/security can add rules.

—Karthik
